summary: Defines two autonomic technical objectives for IPv6 prefix management at the edge of large ISP networks, with an extension for IPv4 prefixes. An important purpose is to validate the design of components of the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: Large networks have to hand out blocks of addresses. This lets the network do much of that sharing by itself.

questions: how can isps automate prefix assignment
what is a grasp prefix objective
subtitle: Automating the distribution of address blocks in large ISP networks.

tldr.problem: Large ISP networks must assign IPv6 prefixes to edge routers efficiently and dynamically as devices join and leave, but current approaches rely heavily on human planning and static configuration.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8992 defines two GRASP objectives and a Prefix Manager ASA that devices use to discover each other and negotiate IPv6 prefix allocation autonomously. A device that runs out of address space requests more from an upstream device through GRASP negotiation.
tldr.outcome: This informational RFC serves as a proof of concept for the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure and provides building blocks for autonomic prefix management; a complete solution requires additional ASA design decisions.

facts.label: Prefix data format
facts.value: 16 bytes for IPv6, 4 bytes for IPv4

today: RFC 8992 is an Informational RFC published in May 2021 that provides a framework and GRASP objectives for autonomic IPv6 prefix management. It remains a proof-of-concept design for validating the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines autonomic IPv6 prefix management for large-scale ISP networks, with an extension supporting IPv4. Its primary purpose is to validate the design of the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure (ANI) and its component protocols.

Although DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD) can automate prefix assignment from one router to another, it requires human planning of which prefix length each device should request. The Autonomic Networking approach allows devices to negotiate prefix allocation dynamically based on their role and current usage.
sections.plainLanguage: This shows how a self-managing network can hand out address blocks. Instead of a person planning everything, routers can ask each other for what they need.

sections.title: The Prefix Management Problem
sections.content:
In large ISP networks, administrators specify a single IPv6 prefix for the whole network and an initial prefix length for each device role. As devices are added and removed and as customers join and leave, manual management becomes inflexible and error-prone. If a device exhausts its assigned address space, the network fails to grow.

The solution must handle the distribution of a total pool of IPv6 address space to edge routers hierarchically. Each router may request additional prefixes from an upstream device, and may provide prefixes to downstream devices. The RFC focuses on edge prefix management; it assumes the network's core infrastructure already has addresses and prefixes assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is that networks need their edge routers to get more addresses as they grow, but planning this by hand is hard and rigid. The solution lets routers ask each other for what they need.

sections.title: The Autonomic Prefix Management Solution
sections.content:
A Prefix Manager ASA runs on each participating device. When a device runs out of address space, its ASA sends a GRASP Discovery message containing a PrefixManager objective to find peers that can provide more space. It then initiates a GRASP negotiation with one of the discovered peers, proposing a desired prefix length.

An ASA that receives a Discovery request for the PrefixManager objective responds if it is capable of providing prefixes. During negotiation, it decides what length of prefix to offer at each step, or it may send a Confirm Waiting message if it needs to negotiate with its own upstream device first. When negotiation succeeds, both ASAs update their local address pools and logging. If negotiation fails, both sides receive appropriate error codes.
sections.plainLanguage: A program in each router asks around to find who can give it more addresses. It negotiates a deal, and if they agree, both routers update their records.

sections.title: Prefix Management Objectives
sections.content:
RFC 8992 defines two GRASP objectives. The PrefixManager objective carries the requested or offered prefix in CDDL format, with fields for the prefix length (0 to 128 bits for IPv6) and optionally the actual prefix bits. The objective also includes a loop count to prevent infinite negotiation loops.

A second objective, PrefixManager.Params, can be flooded to all nodes to communicate the default prefix length for each device role. For example, in an IPRAN (IP Radio Access Network), a Radio Network Controller Site Gateway might default to /34, an Aggregation Site Gateway to /44, and a Cell Site Gateway to /56. This allows devices to autonomously compute reasonable starting points for negotiations.
sections.plainLanguage: One form says 'I want a /48 prefix' and the other says 'here is how big a prefix each type of device should get by default'. Routers fill them out when they negotiate.

sections.title: Integration with Existing Systems
sections.content:
The ANI/GRASP prefix management approach works alongside DHCPv6-PD. For example, ANI/GRASP can manage prefix distribution within a domain while DHCPv6-PD handles delegation to customer devices at the domain edge. Similarly, RADIUS can provide prefixes to client devices. The RFC does not specify the complete solution; it provides the building blocks. ASAs must implement the algorithms for choosing which prefixes to offer, managing spare pools, and detecting address space fragmentation.

All prefix assignments must be logged for audit, security, and compliance purposes, though the logging mechanism is outside the scope of this RFC. A key risk is that distributed prefix allocation might fragment the address space and increase interior routing protocol table sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: This is one piece of a bigger system. Routers can use this for internal negotiation, while DHCPv6 still hands addresses to customers. Everything should be logged to track what was given out.
